findings.title: Missing Expiry Check in execute(BatchedCall) Allows Expired Admin Keys to Execute
findings.description: The execute(BatchedCall) function checks _isOwnerOrAdmin(keyHash) but never calls _checkExpiry(). The _isOwnerOrAdmin() function in KeyManagement.sol only verifies isRegistered and isAdmin; it does not check the key's expiration timestamp. Every other authorization pathway (execute(SignedBatchedCall), validateUserOp, isValidSignature) properly calls _checkExpiry(). An admin key registered with an expiry timestamp continues to execute arbitrary calls via this path after expiration, including registering new permanent admin keys to maintain access indefinitely.

findings.title: GuardedExecutorHook Does Not Validate ETH Value, Allowing Sub-Keys to Drain Native ETH
findings.description: The beforeExecute function in GuardedExecutorHook receives a uint256 value parameter but never validates it. The code contains a TODO comment ('// TODO: check value') confirming this is a known gap. The permission system checks (target, selector) combinations but not the ETH value attached to calls. Any sub-key granted permission to call even a single function on any target can drain the account's entire native ETH balance by setting _call.value to address(account).balance.

findings.title: Reentrancy in _transferFrom with Infinite Native ETH Allowance
findings.description: The _transferFrom function follows checks-effects-interactions for finite allowances. However, when currentAllowance == type(uint256).max, the allowance is never decremented. The ETH transfer sends value to a potentially attacker-controlled recipient, who can reenter transferFromNative. Since the allowance remains at type(uint256).max, each reentrant call passes the check and sends more ETH. A standard nonReentrant modifier using storage mutex will NOT protect against cross-function reentrancy via multicall's delegatecall; transient storage must be used for the reentrancy lock.

findings.title: Hook afterValidateUserOp Completely Overrides Validation Data, Bypassing Key Expiry and Signature Checks
findings.description: When a key has a hook with AFTER_VALIDATE_USER_OP_FLAG, the hook's return value completely replaces the account's computed validationData. This means a hook can remove key expiry restrictions, override signature validation results, or extend the validity window beyond what the key's Settings allow. Additionally, hookData is explicitly documented as unsigned — any UserOp bundler can set arbitrary hookData, and a hook that relies on hookData for authorization decisions is vulnerable to manipulation.

findings.title: Unverified keyHash in executeUserOp Enables Key Substitution via Malicious EntryPoint
findings.description: In executeUserOp, the keyHash is parsed from userOp.signature and used for permission checks in _dispatch without re-verifying that it matches the key validated during validateUserOp. Under the standard ERC-4337 EntryPoint, signature bytes are immutable between validation and execution. However, if updateEntryPoint() sets a custom EntryPoint, this invariant could break, allowing an attacker to validate with one key but execute with different permissions.

findings.title: No Reentrancy Guard in _execute Allows Reentrant Calls via Hook or External Target
findings.description: The _execute function makes three sequential external calls with no reentrancy protection: hook.handleBeforeExecute() (non-view), to.call{value}() (arbitrary external call), and hook.handleAfterExecute() (non-view). Any of these calls can reenter the account. While hooks are admin-configured, a legitimate hook with a subtle vulnerability or one that calls an attacker-controlled oracle could enable nested execution, leaving state from the original execution context stale during reentrant calls.

findings.title: updateEntryPoint Lacks Address Validation, Allowing Malicious EntryPoint to Bypass Security Model
findings.description: updateEntryPoint(address) accepts any address without validation. It can be set to address(0), an EOA, or a malicious contract. A malicious EntryPoint can call validateUserOp and executeUserOp with arbitrary parameters, completely bypassing the account's security model. While this requires admin access, the potentially irreversible and catastrophic nature of the action warrants input validation.

findings.title: msg.value Reuse in Multicall via delegatecall Creates Latent Double-Spend Vulnerability
findings.description: The multicall function is external payable and uses address(this).delegatecall in a loop. msg.value is preserved across all iterations. Currently no function in the codebase references msg.value directly (the execute path uses _call.value from the Call struct), making this a latent vulnerability. However, any future function or hook that trusts msg.value would be immediately exploitable through multicall. This anti-pattern has caused major exploits historically (Opyn hack, SushiSwap Miso).

findings.title: Short Calldata (1-3 bytes) Treated as ANY_FN_SEL Wildcard in GuardedExecutorHook
findings.description: In _canExecute(), calldata of length 1-3 bytes falls through both conditions: data.length >= 4 (false) and data.length == 0 (false). The fnSel variable retains its initialization value of ANY_FN_SEL (0x32323232), conflating short calldata with the wildcard selector constant. This means calls with 1-3 bytes of data are checked against wildcard permissions rather than being handled distinctly, potentially allowing a sub-key with (target, ANY_FN_SEL) permission to send 1-3 byte payloads to trigger the target's fallback.

findings.title: Nonces Not Scoped Per-KeyHash Enables Griefing via Cross-Key Nonce Consumption
findings.description: The nonce key space (upper 192 bits) is global to the account, not scoped per signing key. Different keys sharing the same nonce key space compete for sequence numbers. A holder of one key can front-run another key's signed transaction by consuming the same nonce. SignedBatchedCall correctly includes keyHash in the signed data (preventing key substitution), but the nonce is consumed from the global space in _useNonce without checking which key is using it, enabling griefing/denial-of-service against specific key holders.

findings.title: SettingsLib.isAdmin Extracts 56 Bits Instead of 8, Causing False Admin Positives
findings.description: isAdmin() uses shr(200, settings) in assembly, which shifts the entire uint256 right by 200 bits. This leaves the top 56 bits (7 bytes: 6 'unused' + 1 isAdmin) in the result. The result is assigned to a bool, where any non-zero value is truthy. If any of the upper 6 'unused' bytes contain non-zero data, isAdmin() returns true even if the isAdmin byte is 0, incorrectly granting admin status.

findings.title: Admin Key Can Escalate Privileges Without Restriction by Registering Permanent Admin Keys
findings.description: An admin key can call register() + update() to create additional admin keys with no expiry or hooks. While by design, this means a single compromised admin key can establish permanent persistent access. No timelock, multi-sig, or rate limit protects key management operations, making the blast radius of a compromised admin key equivalent to a compromised root key.

findings.title: TransientAllowance Slot Computation Lacks Domain Separation, Risking Future Collisions
findings.description: The slot computation keccak256(abi.encode(spender)) has no domain separator. Any future module using the same pattern for transient storage would collide. Currently safe as TransientAllowance is the only transient storage user, but this is a latent architectural risk.

findings.title: Zero-Amount Transfer Returns False Instead of Reverting, Creating Silent No-Ops
findings.description: transferFromNative and transferFromNativeTransient return false on zero-amount transfers without reverting. This creates silent no-ops in composed transactions, especially via multicall. The zero-amount check also occurs before the from != address(this) validation, making behavior inconsistent. Callers that do not check return values will silently succeed on zero-amount calls.

findings.title: _isSelfCall Ignores Selector Parameter, Blocking All Self-Calls Regardless of Function
findings.description: _isSelfCall(address to, bytes4) accepts but ignores the selector parameter. The function blocks ALL self-calls regardless of selector. While more restrictive than needed (safe), the dead parameter creates confusion about intended behavior and may prevent legitimate restricted self-calls that should be permitted.

findings.title: Root Key Cannot Be Revoked or Restricted After EOA Private Key Compromise
findings.description: The root key (EOA private key, keyHash = bytes32(0)) is always valid and can never be revoked or restricted. If the EOA private key is compromised, no on-chain action can prevent the attacker from using root key access. This is an inherent limitation of the EIP-7702 delegation model but warrants explicit documentation.

findings.title: invalidateNonce Per-Call Rate Limit Bypassable via Batched Self-Calls
findings.description: The per-call limit of type(uint16).max nonces is trivially bypassable by batching multiple invalidateNonce self-calls in a single BatchedCall. An admin can skip N * 65535 nonces in one transaction, far exceeding the intended per-call limit. The rate limit provides no practical protection against determined nonce space exhaustion.

findings.title: isValidSignature Reverts on Revoked/Expired Keys Instead of Returning ERC-1271 Invalid Magic Value
findings.description: isValidSignature calls getKey(keyHash) which reverts with KeyDoesNotExist() for revoked keys, and _checkExpiry which reverts with KeyExpired() for expired keys. Per ERC-1271, callers expect a bytes4 return value (_1271_INVALID_VALUE), not a revert. Integrating contracts that wrap isValidSignature without try/catch will have their entire transaction revert when an expired or revoked key is used.

findings.title: P256 Signature Malleability: No Low-s Enforcement in KeyLib.verify
findings.description: OpenZeppelin's P256.verify does not enforce low-s values. For any valid P256 signature (r, s), the signature (r, n-s) is also valid. This is mitigated by nonce consumption in execute(SignedBatchedCall) and validateUserOp paths. However, external contracts that rely on P256 signature uniqueness (e.g., using signature hash as a mapping key) could be affected. Note: the webauthn-sol library used for WebAuthnP256 keys DOES enforce low-s.

findings.title: CalldataDecoder.removeSelector Underflows on Short Calldata, Causing Out-of-Gas Revert
findings.description: removeSelector uses assembly sub(data.length, 4) without overflow protection. If data.length < 4, this underflows to a huge value, causing the subsequent abi.decode to read from an enormous memory region and revert with out-of-gas. Only reachable via executeUserOp (line 87), which requires a conforming EntryPoint to send valid calldata, limiting exploitability in the current deployment.

findings.title: WebAuthn requireUV=false Allows Presence-Only Authentication Without Biometric Verification
findings.description: WebAuthn verification uses requireUV: false, meaning only user presence (a tap) is required, not user verification (biometric/PIN). A briefly stolen hardware key can authorize transactions without the owner's biometric confirmation. This reduces the security guarantee of WebAuthnP256 keys to a single factor.

findings.title: WrappedDataHash NatSpec and Code Use Inconsistent EIP-712 Type Strings
findings.description: The code uses the EIP-712 type string 'UniswapWalletMessage(bytes32 data)' while the NatSpec documentation states 'UniswapMinimalDelegationMessage(bytes32 hash)'. Both the type name and field name differ between documentation and implementation. This discrepancy could confuse integrators computing the type hash off-chain.

findings.title: Key Expiration Off-By-One: isExpired Uses <= While ERC-4337 EntryPoint Uses >
findings.description: isExpired uses _exp <= block.timestamp (expired AT the timestamp), while ERC-4337's EntryPoint uses > (expired AFTER the timestamp). Keys expire one second earlier than the EntryPoint would enforce, creating an inconsistency: a key valid in the EntryPoint's view may be rejected by the account's own expiry check at the boundary timestamp.
